extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law and political science
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and explanation of the design choices and functioning of the U.S. federal Constitution, focusing on the executive election system and the national judiciary and the political rationale behind those institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive influence on foreign policy requires a single consistent agent
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power always exercises a great influence upon the foreign policy of the country, for a negotiation cannot be opened or successfully carried on otherwise than by a single agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because foreign policy requires a single, consistent representative, frequent changes in the head of state (as in some elective systems) increase danger and instability; limitations on executive functions reduce but do not eliminate this need for a steady agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective system risk varies with national circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The dangers of the elective system applied to the head of the state are augmented or decreased by the peculiar circumstances of the people which adopts it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a country with few external threats and a populace experienced in freedom (as the United States), a weak/subordinate elective executive may be acceptable; in precarious/exposed nations the elective system for the chief magistrate is more dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a special electoral body rather than let legislature elect the president
rubrics_metrics.description: To delegate the electoral powers of the nation to a body of representatives chosen for that express purpose (special electors) rather than entrust that power to the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: legislators are chosen for longer terms and may be exposed to manoeuvres of corruption before a future presidential election; special electors, like a jury, remain mixed with the crowd until election day and appear solely to give votes, reducing corruption and representing current public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors should vote separately on the same day and transmit sealed votes
rubrics_metrics.description: It was determined that the electors should all vote upon the same day, without being convoked to the same place; votes should be transmitted sealed to the president of the senate and opened and counted in the presence of the senate and the house of representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure reduces prolonged uncertainty and the dangers of assemblies becoming centers of passion and cabal; transmitting sealed individual votes (not just a majority result) preserves the particularity of elector choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple majority decisive; remedy if no electoral majority
rubrics_metrics.description: It was admitted that the simple majority should be decisive; if none of the candidates has a majority of electors, the house of representatives then proceeds immediately to elect the president but must choose one of the three candidates who have the highest numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of a special electoral body and the limit to three candidates for House decision smooths obstacles that are not inherent to the elective system; in the House vote the majority of states (states vote as units) decides, not the majority of members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit House selection to top three electoral candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate has a majority of electoral votes, the house of representatives must fix upon one of the three candidates who have the highest numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting choice to three candidates increases the chance of decisive selection and refers the matter to an enlightened public body, reducing delay and perpetual agitation that accompanies repeated elector balloting or reappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: The election is a national crisis with predictable political effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The period which immediately precedes an election and the moment of its duration must always be considered as a national crisis, perilous in proportion to internal embarrassments and external dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elections intensify passions, factional ardor, and intrigue; the president may prioritize re-election over governing, catering to majority caprices; once the choice is determined a calmer season returns. Electors and parties rally around individuals, making elections the all-engrossing topic before decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-eligibility of the president: trade-off between continuity and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing the president to be re-elected can encourage hope for prolonged administrations (useful in crises) but also greatly increases intrigue and corruption because the chief magistrate can use state resources and influence for electioneering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ineligible again, a president would be less tempted to pander to popular desires; if re-eligible, the president's desire for re-election tends to subordinate public interest, replacing patriotic leadership with adroitness and corrupt influence. Historical practice (Washington declining a third term) functionally limited re-eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design a weak and subordinate executive when circumstances permit
rubrics_metrics.description: Given favorable external circumstances (no hostile neighbours) and a populace experienced in freedom, legislators created a weak and subordinate executive which could without danger be made elective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional choice relies on national conditions—geography, demographics, political culture—to minimize dangers of an elective executive; legislative precautions (electoral college design) complement physical and political securities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government requires national judiciary to enforce laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The great difficulty was not to devise the constitution of the federal government, but to find out a method of enforcing its laws; a federal government stands in greater need of the support of judicial institutions than any other, because it is naturally weak and opposed to formidable opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts provide moral force that substitutes for physical coercion; without federal courts the Union could not reliably compel obedience or repel attacks—state tribunals alone are inadequate because they would be partial or foreign to national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts are inadequate to enforce federal laws due to partiality and multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: To intrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals instituted by the states would be to allow foreign and partial judges to preside over the nation; the number of different state tribunals would produce multiple divergent interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because states have distinct origins, maxims, and interests, relying on their courts would undermine uniform national jurisprudence; multiplicity (thirteen then twenty-four courts deciding without appeal) threatens inconsistent application of federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a federal judiciary with a supreme court and inferior courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire judicial power of the Union was centred in one tribunal denominated the supreme court of the United States, with inferior courts appended to it (district and circuit courts) to facilitate expedition of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferior courts decide small causes without appeal and larger causes with appeal; supreme court holds an annual solemn session; judges of supreme and inferior courts are named by the president with the advice of the senate, their offices are inalienable, and their salaries once fixed should not be altered by the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judges' appointments, tenure, and salary to secure independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of the supreme court are named neither by the people nor the legislature, but by the president of the United States, acting with the advice of the senate; to render them independent their office was made inalienable and their salary, when once fixed, should not be altered by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions aim to insulate federal judges from political pressures so they can enforce federal law impartially; jury was introduced into federal courts in the same manner and cases as in state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court empowered to determine jurisdictional conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: It was necessary to allow one of the courts to judge its own cause; the supreme court of the United States was therefore invested with the right of determining all questions of jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no neutral third tribunal exists between a superior federal court and a superior state court, the federal supreme court must have ultimate authority to decide competency to ensure uniform interpretation of the constitution and federal laws; this limits state sovereignty only by law and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court decides both fact and law (differs from cour de cassation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme court decides upon the evidence of the fact, as well as upon the law of the case, whereas the French cour de cassation only hears appeals and does not pronounce a decision of its own but refers the cause to another tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights substantive powers of the U.S. Supreme Court to render final judgments on both factual and legal questions, strengthening the uniformity of federal jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial moral force substitutes for physical force in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The great end of justice is to substitute the notion of right for that of violence; the authority awarded to the intervention of a court of justice by the general opinion of mankind is so surprisingly great that it gives a bodily influence to the shadow of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral authority of courts makes the use of physical force rare; when physical force is necessary, its power is doubled by association with the idea of law. This is a foundational reason for having an effective judiciary for the Union.
